newsitem.title: EGYPT: Arafat says Israel declares war on Palestinians.
newsitem.headline: Arafat says Israel declares war on Palestinians.

text.p: Palestinian President Yasser Arafat said on Saturday Israel had declared war on Palestinians rather than "terrorism" by a series of measures it took in the wake of a double suicide bombing in west Jerusalem.

Arafat, speaking to reporters after talks with Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak, said U.S. President Bill Clinton must intervene to save the Middle East peace process but that Israel had to have faith in peace in order to overcome the current crisis.

"The Israeli government used this situation and this incident (the suicide bombing) to declare war on the Palestinian people, their National Authority and their leadership instead of declaring it against terrorism," Arafat told reporters after talks with Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's cabinet demanded Arafat crack down on Moslem militants responsible for a double suicide bombing in a Jerusalem market on Wednesday that killed 13 people and wounded 170.

Israel also suspended peace talks with the Palestinian Authority, rounded up scores of suspected militants, closed off the West Bank and Gaza Strip, demanded the extradition of the PLO police chief and threatened to re-enter Palestinian self-rule areas to seize militants if Arafat failed to do the job.

"What is happening is a blow to the peace process as a whole. Israel is declaring war against the Palestinian people. The Israeli government and Netanyahu in particular is striving to chain the peace process," Arafat said.

"The intervention of the American president is necessary in the current circumstances more than any other time before and the only way out of this crisis that the peace process is going through is for the Israeli side to believe in the importance of peace," he added.

Clinton has said he would send special envoy Dennis Ross to the region once the period of mourning in Israel was over and that any visit by Secretary of State Madeleine Albright to the Middle East would only take place after Ross's visit.
U.S. officials had said on Thursday that Albright was seriously considering a visit soon, as a result of Wednesday's bombing incident.
Arafat arrived in Egypt earlier on Saturday and went straight into talks with Mubarak on the crisis in the Middle East peace talks, Egyptian state television said.

"I told President Mubarak about all the dangerous measures announced by Israel after the terrorist operation that happened recently in Jerusalem and which we condemn completely," Arafat said. He has since returned to Gaza.

Arafat described as "collective punishment" the measures taken by Israel since the suicide bombing and said Mubarak told him he would "begin movements on all fronts to decrease the suffering of the Palestinian people," but did not give details.
Egypt has been trying to jump-start Israeli-Palestinian peace talks which collapsed in March after Israel began to build a new Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem.

Arafat, who met Mubarak in the Egyptian leader's private residence in Burg el-Arab, near the Mediterranean city of Alexandria, was accompanied by senior Palestinian officials Saeb Erekat, Nabil Shaath and Mahmoud Abbas.
The Palestinian leader is also under fire from legislators over allegations of rampant corruption and misrule in his administration.
